title: Emission frontier coordination and batching heuristics
body:
Context and motivation:

We continue to get pressure from product/console and early customers for tighter p99 streaming latencies while preserving per-token cost advantages of batching and KV caching. Current runtime separates prefill (KV warmup and attention prefills) and decode (token emission) into pipelines that largely compete for GPU slots and local memory. We have many docs exploring prefills, kv-handshake, slot arbitration; this note attempts to introduce the "emission frontier" concept and outline concrete heuristics and experiments to coordinate prefills and decodes in a way that reduces tail latency without blowing up token cost.

What is the emission frontier?

Define the emission frontier as the set of in-flight streams whose next-decoder-emit is near enough in time that their scheduling decisions materially affect p95/p99 latency. Practically: any stream with remaining prefill or decode work estimated to finish within X ms of each other (X depends on SLO, e.g. 30ms) is on the same frontier. The runtime should treat the frontier as a coordination surface where microbatch composition, kernel choices, and KV residency policies are decided jointly rather than per-request.

Key observations that motivate a frontier approach:

- Prefill work (long KV writes, large attention windows) can be throttled or delayed slightly in favor of imminent short emits and vice versa depending on cost/latency tradeoffs.
- Small emits grouped together can be serviced by a single kernel invocation with lower overhead compared to many tiny decodes if emission alignment is possible.

- Kernel choice (FP32/AMP/quantized-INT8) and execution path has startup cost; grouping streams with similar kernel affinity reduces repeated kernel flips that kill throughput.

- KV cache residency (keep vs evict vs loan) decisions affect future frontier membership — the runtime can preemptively pin KV shards for streams likely to be on the next frontier.

Goals for an emission-frontier scheduler

1) Reduce p95/p99 latency for streaming emits by 15-30% in mixed workloads (short-chatty + long-prefill).
2) Preserve or reduce per-token GPU compute cost relative to current baseline by opportunistic batching and avoiding kernel thrash.
3) Keep fairness between high-priority SLO streams and background bulk workloads; avoid starvation.

High-level design

1) Frontier detection:
   - Maintain soft timers per stream estimating next-emit-time using prompt length, model step time history, and user-level hints (early-emit-only flag).
   - Streams with estimated next-emit within frontier_threshold_ms are flagged frontier=true.
   - frontier_threshold_ms is adaptive: higher under heavy load (to allow bigger batch windows) and lower under slack.

2) Frontier batching window (cohort formation):
   - When frontier set changes, open a small batching window (t_batch_ms) to allow microbatches to align. The window is tiny (e.g., 2-10ms) and configurable per-class.
   - Within window, prefer grouping by kernel_affinity (sequence length, quantization profile), priority class, and KV_hotness.

3) Kernel-affinity hints and sticky kernels:
   - Each stream carries a runtime kernel_hint (e.g., FP16_fast, INT8_cachefriendly). The scheduler attempts to schedule a frontier cohort on the same kernel where possible.
   - If switching kernel incurs >T_switch_ms overhead, scheduler will prefer to combine similar-hint streams even if it means slight latency increase for outliers.
4) Soft priority and fast-lane preemption:
   - Streams may declare priorities (realtime/high, normal, background). High priority streams can preempt background slots within frontier, but preemption is soft: background microbatch will be given a small grace period to finish unless it conflicts with strict SLOs.
   - Preemption should attempt to re-cohere partial microbatches into new microbatches to avoid stranded tokens.

5) KV residency coordination:
   - Frontier coordinator emits short-lived KV pins: for streams likely to re-enter the frontier in the next N emits, we keep KV shards pinned (loan mode) on-GPU for a short TTL.
   - Eviction is aggressive for background streams to reclaim memory for hot frontier cohorts.

6) Backpressure and admission control interplay:
   - Use recent emission success/failure to adapt frontier_threshold_ms and cohort window size; when SLO misses increase, widen windows and prioritize kernel-stable cohorts.

Concrete heuristics (initial implementation)

- frontier_threshold_ms = clamp(2 * median_emit_interval, 8ms, 80ms) per-worker; median_emit_interval measured over last 1k emits.
- t_batch_ms = min( floor(frontier_threshold_ms / 6), 12ms ). Example: if threshold=60ms t_batch=10ms.
- Cohort sorting keys (in order): [priority_class, kernel_hint, kv_hotness_score (0..1), stream_age]
- If cohort size < min_cohort (e.g., 3 streams) and expected kernel_switch_cost > 1.5 * single_emit_cost, delay cohort by t_batch_ms unless a high-priority stream requests immediate emit.
- KV loan TTL = 2 * median_emit_interval but capped at 500ms for memory safety.

Example flows

Flow A — bursty chatty streams:
  - Many short-turn streams all reach next-emit within 10ms -> frontier picks them up, opens 6ms batching window, groups by kernel_hint, issues a single decode kernel invocation with combined microbatch. Result: lower per-token overhead and bounded p99 improvement.

Flow B — long prefill followed by single short emit:
  - Prefill is heavy and would normally occupy a slot; frontier logic recognizes that the stream's next emit is imminent and will either: (a) postpone some prefill housekeeping ops (e.g., lazy KV compaction) until after emit, or (b) loan some KV shards from background caches rather than evicting, to expedite decode.

Flow C — mixed background bulk + high-priority low-latency streams:
  - High-priority frontier cohort gets front-loaded; background microbatches are allowed to drain but are paused if they would delay high-priority cohort beyond p99 budget.

Metric plan and benchmarks

Metrics to track for each experiment run:
  - p50/p95/p99 emit latency (per-priority class)
  - per-token GPU compute (ms/GPU-token) and kernel-switch frequency
  - KV pin rate, eviction rate, memory pressure events
  - Microbatch size distribution and stranded-token counts (tokens queued but not executed in batch)
  - Fairness metrics: tail-latency regression for background class

Benchmark scenarios (minimally):
  - Synthetic mix: 60% short-chatty (turn length 8–24 tokens), 30% medium-prefill (prefill length 512 tokens), 10% large-batch offline bursts. Vary concurrency from 50 to 800 streams.
  - Real trace replay: sample from production chat traces (with PII stripped) for 1h windows.

Experiment rollout plan

1) Canary on single worker pool with controlled load generator (AB test against baseline admission control) — 2 weeks.
2) Expand to multi-pool with kernel-stable workers enabled — measure kernel-switch delta — 3 weeks.
3) Limited customer beta with opt-in real-time flag in console — collect feedback and real traces — 4 weeks.

Risks and mitigations

- Risk: Frontier coordination increases coordination/timer overhead and may itself add micro-latency. Mitigation: keep windows tiny; implement in fast-path C++ loop; fall back to simple scheduling if overhead>benefit.
- Risk: KV pin TTL miscalculation can cause OOM on GPU. Mitigation: enforce strict per-worker KV memory cap and preempt pins under pressure.
- Risk: Starvation of background workloads. Mitigation: incorporate fairness tokens and ensure each worker reserves a small fraction of capacity for background microbatches.

Open questions / next steps

- What exact kernel_switch_cost threshold justifies grouping vs immediate execution? Need microbench across hardware variants (A100, H100, T4 emulation).
- How to best expose user-level hints (e.g., emit_urgency) in the public API without encouraging brittle client-side heuristics?
- Should frontier logic be centralized (global coordinator) or fully localized per-worker for scalability? Start local and evaluate cross-worker coherence issues.

Action items

- Proto: Jonah to implement frontier detection and tiny batching window in the scheduler (proto branch: feat/frontier-proto). (2 weeks)
- Microbench: Priya to produce kernel-switch microbench across model configs and hardware. (1 week)
- Integration: Ethan to add KV loan TTL wiring and safe-eviction hooks. (2 weeks)
- Metrics: Aisha to add dashboarding for the metrics listed above and prepare AB test harness. (1 week)

References and context links:

- See linked Linear ticket for experiment plan and workload generator.
- Related notes: crossphase-kv-handshake, microbatching-priority-heuristics (existing docs) — this doc intentionally focuses on the coordination surface rather than internal KV serialization.

Notes to self: keep simulations reproducible; instrument emit_time estimates carefully. We'll iterate on cohort keys after first canary.

End of draft.
